scan.note: Generated by 'aws-security-audit demo' against a moto mock account (123456789012). This is not a real AWS account and no real AWS API calls were made.

checks.title: Root user has MFA enabled
checks.description: Without MFA, the root user is protected by a password alone.

checks.title: No bucket policy allows access to anyone
checks.description: A bucket policy statement that allows Principal '*' with no Condition lets anyone on the internet perform the listed actions, unless RestrictPublicBuckets is on.

checks.title: A multi-region CloudTrail trail is logging all management events
checks.description: Without a trail covering every region there is no record of who did what, including in regions you do not use, which is exactly where an attacker would go.

checks.title: No AMIs or EBS snapshots are shared publicly
checks.description: A public AMI or snapshot can be copied by any AWS account. Disk images often contain credentials, keys and data that were never meant to leave the account.

checks.title: No security group opens admin or database ports to the internet
checks.description: Inbound rules from 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 to SSH, RDP or common database ports invite brute force and exploit attempts within minutes. CIS 5.2/5.3 are attached per finding, only when an admin port is exposed over IPv4 or IPv6 respectively.

checks.title: No IAM user has full admin attached directly
checks.description: Users with AdministratorAccess or a '*:*' policy attached directly are hard to audit and, if their keys leak, give away the whole account.

checks.title: IAM users with a console password have MFA
checks.description: A console password without MFA can be phished or guessed.

checks.title: RDS instances are not publicly accessible
checks.description: A publicly accessible instance gets a public DNS name and IP. Whether it is actually reachable also depends on its security groups and subnet routes, which this check does not evaluate.

checks.title: S3 Block Public Access is on for the account
checks.description: The account-level Block Public Access settings stop any bucket in the account being made public by an ACL or bucket policy, whatever its own settings say.

checks.title: CloudTrail logs are encrypted with a KMS key
checks.description: SSE-KMS adds a second permission check: reading the logs needs kms:Decrypt on the key as well as access to the bucket, and every decrypt is itself logged.

checks.title: CloudTrail log file validation is on
checks.description: Validation writes signed digest files, so you can prove later that log files were not altered or deleted.

checks.title: AWS Config is recording all resource types in every region
checks.description: AWS Config keeps a history of how each resource was configured, which is what you need to answer 'when did this security group open port 22?' during an incident. CIS also expects global resource types (IAM) to be recorded in one region; that part is shown in the evidence but not enforced per region.

checks.title: Default security groups have no rules and are not in use
checks.description: Anything launched without a chosen security group lands in the VPC's default group. If that group allows traffic, those resources are reachable without anyone deciding they should be. A default group with rules fails (CIS 5.4); one with no rules but attached interfaces gets a low finding.

checks.title: EBS encryption by default is on in every region
checks.description: With this on, every new EBS volume and snapshot copy in the region is encrypted automatically.

checks.title: EC2 instances require IMDSv2
checks.description: IMDSv1 answers plain GET requests, so a server-side request forgery bug in an app on the instance can be used to read the instance role's credentials. IMDSv2 needs a session token.

checks.title: GuardDuty is enabled in every region
checks.description: GuardDuty watches CloudTrail, VPC flow logs and DNS logs for signs of compromise, such as credentials used from unusual places or instances talking to known bad hosts.

checks.title: Password policy requires 14+ characters and prevents reuse
checks.description: Short or reused passwords are easier to guess or to replay from another breach.

checks.title: Customer managed KMS keys have automatic rotation on
checks.description: Rotation creates new key material on a schedule and keeps the old material for decryption, which limits how much data any one version of the key protects. Only enabled, symmetric, customer managed keys with AWS-generated material support it, so only those are checked.

checks.title: RDS instances have encrypted storage
checks.description: Encryption at rest protects the data files, backups, snapshots and read replicas.

checks.title: Each bucket is covered by Block Public Access
checks.description: S3 applies the stricter of the bucket and account settings. A bucket passes if, for each of the four settings, either the bucket or the account has it on.

checks.title: Buckets have default encryption configured
checks.description: Since January 2023 AWS applies SSE-S3 to new buckets automatically, so on current accounts this mostly reports which algorithm each bucket uses. It fails if no default encryption is configured.

checks.title: Buckets have versioning and server access logging
checks.description: Versioning lets you recover objects that were overwritten or deleted, including by ransomware or a bad script. Server access logs record who requested what. Each bucket gets one finding for versioning and one for logging.

checks.title: Root user has no access keys
checks.description: Access keys on the root user give unrestricted, unscoped API access to the whole account.

checks.title: Active access keys are rotated within 90 days
checks.description: Long-lived keys build up exposure: the older a key, the more places it may have leaked to.

checks.title: Credentials unused for 45 days are disabled
checks.description: Passwords and keys nobody uses are pure risk: they can still be stolen but nobody would notice.

findings.title: Root user has MFA enabled
findings.message: MFA is not enabled for the root user

remediation.console: Sign in as the root user, open Security credentials from the account menu, and choose Assign MFA device. A hardware key or passkey is the stronger choice.
remediation.cli: Root MFA has to be set up while signed in as the root user; use the console steps.

findings.title: No bucket policy allows access to anyone
findings.message: Bucket demo-public-assets policy allows access to anyone (Principal '*')

remediation.console: S3 > choose the bucket > Permissions > Bucket policy > Edit. Replace Principal '*' with the accounts or roles that need access, or add a Condition. For a public website, serve it through CloudFront with origin access control instead.
remediation.cli:
aws s3api get-bucket-policy --bucket <BUCKET> --query Policy --output text > policy.json
# edit policy.json, then:
aws s3api put-bucket-policy --bucket <BUCKET> --policy file://policy.json
# or remove it entirely: aws s3api delete-bucket-policy --bucket <BUCKET>

findings.title: A multi-region CloudTrail trail is logging all management events
findings.message: No multi-region trail is fully logging management events (org-audit: logging is stopped)

remediation.console: CloudTrail > Trails > Create trail. Apply it to all regions (the default for new trails), log read and write management events, and send logs to a dedicated S3 bucket. If a trail exists but is stopped, open it and choose Start logging.
remediation.cli:
aws cloudtrail create-trail --name <TRAIL> --s3-bucket-name <BUCKET> --is-multi-region-trail --enable-log-file-validation --kms-key-id <KMS_KEY_ARN>
aws cloudtrail start-logging --name <TRAIL>

findings.title: No AMIs or EBS snapshots are shared publicly
findings.message: EBS snapshot snap-41765208fbfae3989 is public

remediation.console: EC2 > AMIs > choose the AMI > Actions > Edit AMI permissions > Private. EC2 > Snapshots > choose the snapshot > Actions > Snapshot settings > Modify permissions > Private. Then turn on 'Block public access' for AMIs and for EBS snapshots in EC2 > Settings.
remediation.cli:
aws ec2 modify-image-attribute --image-id <AMI_ID> --launch-permission 'Remove=[{Group=all}]'
aws ec2 modify-snapshot-attribute --snapshot-id <SNAPSHOT_ID> --attribute createVolumePermission --operation-type remove --group-names all
aws ec2 enable-image-block-public-access --image-block-public-access-state block-new-sharing
aws ec2 enable-snapshot-block-public-access --state block-all-sharing

findings.title: No security group opens admin or database ports to the internet
findings.message: Security group sg-b3efeebac5e70869f (reporting-db) allows MySQL/MariaDB (3306) from 0.0.0.0/0

remediation.console: EC2 > Security Groups > choose the group > Inbound rules > Edit inbound rules. Remove the 0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0 rules for these ports. Reach instances through Systems Manager Session Manager or a VPN, and allow databases only from the application's security group.
remediation.cli:
aws ec2 revoke-security-group-ingress --group-id <SG_ID> --ip-permissions 'IpProtocol=tcp,FromPort=<PORT>,ToPort=<PORT>,IpRanges=[{CidrIp=0.0.0.0/0}]'
aws ec2 revoke-security-group-ingress --group-id <SG_ID> --ip-permissions 'IpProtocol=tcp,FromPort=<PORT>,ToPort=<PORT>,Ipv6Ranges=[{CidrIpv6=::/0}]'

findings.title: No IAM user has full admin attached directly
findings.message: User deploy-bot has full admin attached directly: ci-deploy-everything (customer managed, allows *:*)

remediation.console: IAM > Users > choose the user > Permissions. Remove the admin policy and grant what the user needs through a group or a role they assume, ideally with MFA required.
remediation.cli:
aws iam detach-user-policy --user-name <USER> --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess
aws iam delete-user-policy --user-name <USER> --policy-name <INLINE_POLICY>

findings.title: IAM users with a console password have MFA
findings.message: User alice has a console password but no MFA device

remediation.console: IAM > Users > choose the user > Security credentials > Assign MFA device. If the user does not need the console, remove the console password instead.
remediation.cli:
aws iam create-virtual-mfa-device --virtual-mfa-device-name <USER> --outfile <USER>-qr.png --bootstrap-method QRCodePNG
aws iam enable-mfa-device --user-name <USER> --serial-number arn:aws:iam::<ACCOUNT_ID>:mfa/<USER> --authentication-code1 <CODE1> --authentication-code2 <CODE2>
Or, if console access is not needed: aws iam delete-login-profile --user-name <USER>

findings.title: AWS Config is recording all resource types in every region
findings.message: AWS Config has no configuration recorder in us-east-1

remediation.console: AWS Config (in the region) > Settings > Edit. Record all resource types, choose a delivery bucket and make sure recording is on.
remediation.cli:
aws configservice put-configuration-recorder --configuration-recorder name=default,roleARN=<CONFIG_ROLE_ARN> --recording-group allSupported=true,includeGlobalResourceTypes=true

findings.title: Default security groups have no rules and are not in use
findings.message: Default security group sg-41660da435c082039 in vpc-4fc78db3064fee8be has 0 inbound and 1 outbound rule(s)

remediation.console: VPC > Security groups > the group named 'default' > remove every inbound and outbound rule. Move any instances or interfaces using it onto purpose-built security groups first.
remediation.cli:
aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids <SG_ID>   # copy the rules to revoke
aws ec2 revoke-security-group-ingress --group-id <SG_ID> --ip-permissions '<INBOUND_RULES_JSON>'
aws ec2 revoke-security-group-egress --group-id <SG_ID> --ip-permissions 'IpProtocol=-1,IpRanges=[{CidrIp=0.0.0.0/0}]'
aws ec2 modify-network-interface-attribute --network-interface-id <ENI_ID> --groups <OTHER_SG_ID>

findings.title: RDS instances have encrypted storage
findings.message: RDS instance orders-db storage is not encrypted

remediation.console: Encryption cannot be turned on for an existing instance. Take a snapshot, copy it with encryption enabled (RDS > Snapshots > Actions > Copy snapshot), restore a new instance from the encrypted copy, then move traffic over.
remediation.cli:
aws rds create-db-snapshot --db-instance-identifier <DB_ID> --db-snapshot-identifier <DB_ID>-plain
aws rds copy-db-snapshot --source-db-snapshot-identifier <DB_ID>-plain --target-db-snapshot-identifier <DB_ID>-encrypted --kms-key-id <KMS_KEY_ID>
aws rds restore-db-instance-from-db-snapshot --db-instance-identifier <NEW_DB_ID> --db-snapshot-identifier <DB_ID>-encrypted
